report.title: Activity: Review and complete a sample size calculation report

segments.text: Adults with chronic pain will be individually randomized in equal groups to novel or standard treatment. Pain relief at four weeks is the primary binary outcome.
segments.explanation: This identifies the population, comparison, allocation and primary outcome with its assessment time.

segments.text: For 70% versus 30% relief, a two-sided 5% test and 90% power require 56 analyzable patients per group.
segments.explanation: The requirement of 56 per group uses 60% versus 30%, a target difference of 30 percentage points. The pilot observed 70% versus 30%; those observations need to be distinguished from the inputs selected for the new calculation.

segments.text: The planned power gives a 90% probability that the novel treatment works.
segments.explanation: Power is the probability that the planned test rejects the null when the specified population difference and other assumptions hold. Here it is evaluated at a 30-percentage-point difference.

segments.text: The total analyzable sample is therefore 56.
segments.explanation: There are two groups: 56 analyzable patients per group means 112 in total. Both counts should appear in the report.

segments.text: To allow for 5% missing outcomes, adding 5% and rounding down gives 58 recruits per group.
segments.explanation: The retained fraction is 0.95. Dividing 56 by 0.95 and rounding upward gives 59 recruits per group, or 118 in total. The analyzable requirement remains 56 per group.

segments.text: Standard care has an 80% discharge percentage
segments.explanation: This is the stated baseline for all three plans. Keeping it fixed makes the target differences comparable.

segments.text: A 20% relative increase in Plan A gives 100% discharged
segments.explanation: A relative increase of 20% gives 80% x 1.20 = 96%, an increase of 16 percentage points. Adding 20 percentage points would give 100%.

segments.text: Plan B's increase of 10 percentage points gives 90% discharged
segments.explanation: Adding 10 percentage points to 80% gives 90%. This is an absolute change.

segments.text: At the same 80% power, Plan B needs fewer patients than Plan A
segments.explanation: In these plans, detecting the smaller 10-point difference in Plan B requires more patients than detecting the 16-point difference in Plan A. The calculation also uses the two event percentages.

segments.text: Increasing power to 90% in Plan C reduces the required sample
segments.explanation: Plan C retains Plan A's event percentages and Type I error probability. Achieving the higher power requires more patients.

segments.text: For 56 analyzable patients per group and 5% expected missing outcomes, we plan to recruit 59 per group
segments.explanation: Dividing 56 by 0.95 and rounding upward gives 59 recruits per group. Actual retention can vary.

segments.text: Anyone who switches treatment will automatically count as lost to follow-up
segments.explanation: A participant who switches treatment can still provide the four-week pain-relief outcome. For the effect of treatment assignment, that outcome remains in the participant's randomized group. Figure 3.1 shows treatment received and outcome availability separately.

segments.text: If expected losses are 10% in one group and 20% in the other, an overall 15% allowance will meet the expected analyzable requirement in both groups
segments.explanation: The groups need separate retention assumptions. For 56 analyzable patients, the recruitment calculations give 63 at 10% expected loss and 70 at 20%. With equal recruitment, the app uses 70 per group so that the higher-loss group meets the expected requirement.

segments.text: Recruiting extra participants will remove bias caused by missing outcomes
segments.explanation: Extra recruitment can protect the expected count. Missing-outcome bias depends on why outcomes are missing and how they are analyzed. Prevention, appropriate analysis and sensitivity analyses remain necessary.

segments.text: For a target mean difference of 3 units and an SD of 5, Cohen's d is 0.60
segments.explanation: For this independent two-group comparison, d = 3 / 5 = 0.60.

segments.text: The corresponding two-group ANOVA therefore uses f = 0.60
segments.explanation: For the stated unadjusted comparison with two equally sized groups, f = d / 2 = 0.30. Entering f = 0.60 represents a mean difference of 6 units at SD 5.

segments.text: A software result labeled total sample size can be recorded as patients per group
segments.explanation: The output label determines what the count represents. For two equally sized groups, the total is twice the per-group count. The final report should state both counts explicitly.

segments.text: Selecting this unadjusted ANOVA automatically accounts for baseline pain scores
segments.explanation: Baseline-adjusted analysis requires a method and assumptions for the intended covariate adjustment. The simple two-group ANOVA calculation here contains no baseline covariate.
